post.caption: Marcasite jewelry contains no marcasite. The sparkly stones are really pyrite, also called fool's gold. Both minerals are iron sulfide with the same formula, but their atoms are arranged differently, so their crystals differ. Real marcasite can crumble into powder in humid air, and museums keep real marcasite in dry rooms. Jewelers cut tiny faceted pieces of pyrite and set them in silver. Pyrite's name means fire, since it makes sparks against steel, and wheellock guns used pyrite to make sparks. In Georgian times, pyrite pieces stood in for diamonds. Pre-Columbian artists made mirrors from cut pyrite pieces.
